transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Natarajan (Redwood); Carlos Mendez, Aisha Khan, Samir Patel, Maya Wu (Acme)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey folks, thanks for joining, um we wanted to run through the SDK quickstart and the typical auth story and env setup, and then show a quick python and ts demo. is that still the agenda?
[00:08] Carlos Mendez: yep that works, thanks Jordan. we mainly want to know how hard it is to get running in our staging, and what changes if we go Dedicated.
[00:15] Jordan Lee: cool, priya is gonna do the deep dive on the code bits. priya, do you want to start with auth?
[00:20] Priya Natarajan: yeah sure. so Redwood supports simple API key auth for the hosted API. you set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var locally or in your container and the SDK picks it up. in the quickstart repo we include .env.example with REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_BASE_URL (for private / staging) and optional REDWOOD_MODEL to pin versions.
[00:40] Aisha Khan: is that key scoped? like can we restrict to read-only or per-route?
[00:45] Priya Natarajan: good question. hosted keys can be scoped by project and role via the Console. we also have key rotation and short-lived tokens for CI, and if you run Private you can integrate with your KMS and issue short-lived tokens from your auth system.
[00:58] Samir Patel: for Private deployments, how does KMS work? we use AWS KMS and YubiHSM in some places.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: we support AWS KMS integrations and customer-managed HSM workflows; we'll send the SOC2 and HSM/KMS integration notes - that's one of the follow-ups. for the quick demo, i'm going to switch to the python quickstart.
[01:20] Priya Natarajan: ok opening the repo, it's in examples/quickstarts/python. main file is quickstart.py, very minimal. we import redwood from the SDK, set client = Redwood(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), base_url=os.getenv('REDWOOD_BASE_URL', 'https://api.redwood.ai')) and then call client.generate(...) for text or client.chat.create for chat.
[01:40] Maya Wu: are there typed clients for TS too? our frontend team is TS heavy.
[01:45] Priya Natarajan: yes we have an official TypeScript/Node SDK. the quickstart has an examples/ts folder. snippet: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, baseUrl: process.env.REDWOOD_BASE_URL }); const resp = await client.text.generate({ model: 'redwood-1.0', prompt: '...' });
[02:05] Carlos Mendez: what's the difference in behavior if base_url points to a private control plane?
[02:10] Priya Natarajan: base_url just points the SDK at whatever control plane you have, hosted or private. auth works the same but the backend enforces network controls. for Private, customers often run with VPC peering and private DNS - we provide config docs.
[02:24] Samir Patel: okay and audit logs - are request/response logs kept?
[02:28] Jordan Lee: yes audit logs are available in the Console and via export APIs; for Private you control retention. we'll include that in the security pack we send.
[02:36] Priya Natarajan: coming back to local dev, we recommend setting a small local mock or using Redwood's dev token to avoid hitting prod. our quickstart includes a docker-compose for local env that spins up a small stub that returns canned responses for offline testing.
[02:55] Aisha Khan: that's useful - can we run CI without shipping the key?
[02:59] Priya Natarajan: yep, we suggest using short-lived CI tokens or Vault injected secrets. the quickstart contains an example github action that pulls a secret and runs tests against a staging endpoint.
[03:12] Jordan Lee: i'd like to demo a small end-to-end. Priya, run the python example and then the TS one.
[03:18] Priya Natarajan: running quickstart.py... (typing) output: "Generated text: 'Welcome to Acme Payments sandbox'". the code prints latency and token cost in the response metadata - the SDK surfaces per-token cost estimate which is handy for Optimize integration.
[03:36] Carlos Mendez: where does that cost info come from?
[03:38] Priya Natarajan: that's from the runtime; the response includes token_count and estimated_cost_usd if you're on Hosted. for Dedicated that field can be disabled or mapped to your internal pricing.
[03:48] Maya Wu: and does the SDK support streaming in TS? we have a streaming UX for chat.
[03:52] Priya Natarajan: yes, both SDKs support streaming. in Node we expose an async iterator: for await (const chunk of client.chat.stream(...)) { /* render chunk */ }. python has an event stream as well. there are examples in the quickstart.
[04:08] Samir Patel: about Dedicated - what changes operationally? autoscale? isolation?
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity, predictable throughput, VPC options and stricter network isolation. Shared Hosted is faster to get started but has multi-tenant resource limits and different SLAs. for POC we usually start hosted then spin up dedicated if you need throughput guarantees.
[04:30] Carlos Mendez: perf is key for us. can we benchmark token/sec and p99 latency?
[04:34] Priya Natarajan: absolutely. we'll run a perf harness - we'll need your sample payloads and target QPS. Priya: i'll outline the benchmark steps in the plan.
[04:42] (brief cross talk)
[05:00] Priya Natarajan: quick note: if you use prefix caching or KV-cache for chat, that can drastically cut cost for repeated flows. in the quickstart there's an example using conversation ids and caching keys. sometimes transcribers write it as K V cache so you might see both in docs.
[05:20] Aisha Khan: what's the recommended quantization profile? we like fp16 on GPUs but need lower memory for big models.
[05:26] Priya Natarajan: Optimize suggests quantization per workload; for throughput-oriented workloads int8 or q4 can give big savings. we'll share recommended profiles with the quickstart.
[05:36] Jordan Lee: i'm going to show the Console quickly - open the project page, api keys tab, create key, set role. you can also view per-route costs, traces and token-level breakdowns.
[05:50] (screen share noise)
[06:10] Priya Natarajan: note on error handling: SDK surfaces structured errors with codes like RATE_LIMIT, MODEL_NOT_AVAILABLE, and FALLBACK_TRIGGERED. we recommend implementing an automatic fallback sequence: try low-latency model variant, then degrade to caching or a cheaper model. quickstart includes a helper for that.
[06:28] Carlos Mendez: our compliance team will want the flow for data residency and redaction.
[06:32] Jordan Lee: for Hosted we have region controls; data residency options and retention settings are in Console. for Private it's under your control and we can map logs to your SIEM. we'll attach the compliance docs.
[06:46] Samir Patel: do you support SAML SSO and RBAC for Console?
[06:50] Jordan Lee: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC and granular RBAC. again we'll send the admin guide.
[07:00] Priya Natarajan: returning to the SDK, one more note: the Python SDK supports sync and async usage, and the TypeScript SDK has both promise and streaming APIs. examples in the quickstart show both patterns.
[07:14] Maya Wu: if we want a private deployment, what's the typical lead time?
[07:18] Jordan Lee: depends on scale and integrations; for a standard VPC Private deployment with KMS integration it can be 4-8 weeks. Dedicated reservation is faster for throughput-only needs.
[07:30] Aisha Khan: cost - any rule of thumb for hosted token price vs dedicated?
[07:34] Jordan Lee: hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is contract-based with lower unit costs at scale. we'll include a sample pricing sheet for both so you can model.
[07:45] (pause)
[08:00] Priya Natarajan: i want to walk through the ts quickstart. open examples/ts, index.ts. main bits: import { Redwood } from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const out = await client.chat.create({ model: 'redwood-chat-1', messages: [...] }); console.log(out.text);
[08:25] Carlos Mendez: great. can the SDK be instrumented with OpenTelemetry?
[08:29] Priya Natarajan: yes there's middleware for OTel and we emit trace IDs you can correlate with your APM. instructions are in the repo.
[08:40] Samir Patel: after the perf run, will you help interpret the p99 and throughput?
[08:45] Jordan Lee: yes Priya will run through the results and suggest batching, caching or quantization changes via Redwood Optimize. Optimize can also suggest batch sizes and cache policies based on traces.
[08:58] Aisha Khan: what about rate limits? we have bursty traffic.
[09:02] Priya Natarajan: we support per-project rate limits and token-level throttling. Dedicated gives you higher bursts and configurable autoscaling policies. there's a console page for that.
[09:12] Jordan Lee: small gotcha - when switching models mid-rollout, the SDK will warn you if tokenization differs; you can enable automatic fallback to previous variant to avoid regressions.
[09:26] (some typing sounds)
[09:40] Carlos Mendez: ok let's recap and next steps.
[09:45] Jordan Lee: recap: we'll send the quickstart repo, sample env vars, security pack (SOC2 + KMS notes), and a benchmark plan. Acme will provide sample payloads and throughput targets. we'll aim to run the perf test next week.
[09:59] Aisha Khan: sounds good. one ask - can you provide an example github action that runs tests with ephemeral tokens?
[10:04] Priya Natarajan: yes that's in the quickstart under .github/workflows/ci.yml. we'll point you to it.
[10:12] Samir Patel: please include the HSM integration docs and any compliance exceptions.
[10:16] Jordan Lee: noted. i'll follow up. thanks everyone.
[10:22] (meeting ends, small chatter)

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-hearings: e.g., 'K V cache' sometimes written as 'KV cache', 'redwood-ai' as 'red wood', and some speaker labels defaulted to Speaker 2 in the raw output.

References shared: quickstart repo (link sent by Jordan in chat), security pack (SOC2 + KMS notes), benchmark spreadsheet (template).
